chunks: Muhammad ibn Ali ibn Mahbub from Ya'qub ibn Yazid from Marwak ibn Ubayd from Nashit ibn Salih from Abu al-Hasan (the First), peace be upon him, who said:

I said to him: 'A man from us prays his prayer inside his house, closing its door, then he goes out and prays with his neighbors. Does that prayer, which he prayed alone in his house, count as a congregational prayer?'

He said: 'The one who prays in his house, Allah multiplies for him double the reward of the congregation; he will have fifty degrees. And the one who prays with his neighbors, Allah writes for him the reward of one who prayed behind the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family), and he enters with them in their prayer, so his sins are transferred to them, and he departs with their good deeds.'

key_terms.ضِعْفَيْ أَجْرِ الْجَمَاعَةِ: double the reward of the congregation
key_terms.يَخْرُجُ بِحَسَنَاتِهِمْ: he departs with their good deeds
key_terms.يُخَلِّفُ عَلَيْهِمْ ذُنُوبَهُ: he transfers his sins to them

ai.seo_question: What is the difference in reward and spiritual consequence between praying alone at home and praying with neighbors in Shia hadith?
ai.summary: In this hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Imam al-Rida (AS) distinguishes between the general virtue of private devotion and the specific communal merit of leading one's household or neighbors. While praying alone at home yields fifty degrees of reward, joining neighbors in congregation grants the unique status of following the Prophet, characterized by a spiritual exchange where the leader absorbs the followers' sins and departs with their good deeds. This highlights the Shia emphasis on the leader's role in communal purification and the high value placed on both individual piety and social cohesion in worship.
